data.title: Thailand must halt imminent forcible return of two Uyghur men to China, says Amnesty
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Thailand must halt imminent forcible return of two Uyghur men to China, says Amnesty
Responding to reports that two Uyghur men recently moved to an Immigration Detention Centre in Thailand face imminent forcible deportation to China, Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnès Callamard said:
“Thai authorities must immediately halt any plans to forcibly return these two Uyghur men to China, where they face a real risk of torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance. Thailand must not repeat last year's unlawful deportation of 40 Uyghurs, who were forced back to danger in China.
“These two men fled persecution only to spend more than a decade detained in Thailand. Amnesty International has documented crimes against humanity against Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang. Returning them would expose them to the abuses they sought to escape.
"Both men have previously made clear to their legal representatives that they fear for their lives if returned to China and do not consent to being sent back. Thai authorities must now allow them access to a lawyer of their choice and, together with the international community, urgently find a safe and voluntary third-country solution for them and the other Uyghurs still detained in Thailand.
“No amount of diplomatic assurance from China can override Thailand’s obligations not to return anyone to a real risk of torture or other serious human rights violations. After more than a decade in detention, these men must be released and given the chance to rebuild their lives in safety and freedom "
Background The two men are among five Uyghurs remaining in Thailand from a group of over 300 who were apprehended without charge by the Thai authorities on 13 March 2014 after they had fled persecution and discrimination in China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.

data.title: Human Rights Foundation condemns sentencing of Anon Nampa
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Human Rights Foundation condemns sentencing of Anon Nampa
The Human Rights Foundation (HRF) has issued a statement condemning the sentencing of human rights lawyer Anon Nampa to an additional 2 years and 8 months in prison on a royal defamation charge and calls for the unconditional and immediate release of Anon and other prisoners of conscience. On 30 October Anon and four other activists were found guilty of royal defamation over speeches given at a protest on 25 November 2020 and sentenced to 2 years and 8 months in prison. Anon is now facing a cumulative prison sentence of 34 years and 5 months. According to Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR), 33 people are currently detained on a royal defamation charge, 12 of whom are detained pending trial or appeal. The full statement reads: HRF strongly condemns the Thai court’s sentencing of human rights lawyer Anon Nampa to an additional two years and eight months in prison under the country’s royal defamation law (Article 112 of the Criminal Code) for criticizing the monarchy, bringing his total prison sentence to more than 34 years.
Anon is among more than 290 people who have been charged under the royal defamation law since the youth-led protests that began in 2020. He was among the first prominent figures to publicly challenge the longstanding taboo surrounding discussion of the monarchy in Thai https://ow.ly/cc6p5103VJq
The Thai regime has increasingly weaponized the royal defamation law to suppress freedom of dissent. Dozens remain detained, while others have been forced into exile. According to HRF's Tyranny Tracker, Thailand is ruled by a hybrid authoritarian regime, with civic space continuing to shrink. https://ow.ly/gifF5103VJp
HRF calls on the Thai regime for the unconditional and immediate release of Arnon Nampa and other prisoners of conscience. HRF also calls on Thailand to repeal Article 112 of the Criminal Code and bring its practices in line with international human rights law. See less

data.title: Appeal Court dismisses chicken farm company’s lawsuit against human rights defenders
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Appeal Court dismisses chicken farm company’s lawsuit against human rights defenders
The Appeal Court has dismissed a defamation lawsuit filed by the chicken farm company Thammakaset against three human rights defenders for social media posts about abuse of migrant workers at its farm.
The company filed criminal defamation complaints in 2019 against Angkhana Neelapaijit, Puttanee Kangkun, and Thanaporn Saleephol for sharing and posting on social media in support of migrant workers who reported poor working conditions and other human rights defenders who had been sued by the company.
In August 2023, the South Bangkok Criminal Court dismissed the lawsuit on the grounds that the posts were not about the company but expressed support for other advocates being sued by the company, while a video linked to the posts was found in another case to not be defamatory.
According to the Community Resource Centre Foundation (CRC), the Appeal Court ruled on 2 November to uphold the dismissal on the grounds that the defendants were exercising their right to freedom of expression about a public issue and defending human rights. It noted that the posts were not defamatory towards the company and that the business losses that the company claimed were not a direct result of the posts.
The lawsuits against Angkhana, Puttanee, and Thanaporn are among the over 30 civil and criminal cases filed by the company against human rights defenders, journalists, and workers since 2016 after 14 migrant workers from Myanmar submitted a petition to the National Human Rights Commission claiming that they were made to work for wages that were below-he legal minimum without overtime pay and that their documents had been confiscated by their employer.
The workers were sued by the company in October 2019 for defamation, but later acquitted.

data.title: Court concludes hearings in defamation case against Prachatai, verdict set for 25 Nov
data.author: eng editor 3
data.summary:
Court concludes hearings in defamation case against Prachatai, verdict set for 25 Nov
The Criminal Court has concluded hearings in the defamation case filed against Prachatai by the company that produced the “2475 Dawn of Revolution” Animation. The verdict is scheduled to be delivered on 25 November.
Nakraphiwat, the producer of “2475 Dawn of Revolution,” filed a defamation lawsuit against Prachatai, its former editor-in-chief, and three other people, claiming that its news article of March 2024 contained false information about the company’s relationship with the Army.
Launched on 9 March 2024 and later released online, the animation was produced by Nakra Studio with the copyright owned by Nakraphiwat Co Ltd. After its release, the animation was criticized by pro-democracy netizens for misinterpreting the events of 1932 and for painting those behind the revolution in a bad light.
There were also reports that several army units were screening the animation to conscripts and officers, including the 2 nd Signal Regiment, whose Facebook page reported that the animation was screened to soldiers in the Regiment and their families to raise the “right awareness” about the revolution and build a “love of the nation, religion, and King.”
The lawsuit stems from a report on 15 March 2024 by Prachatai that, according to the analysis of the Anti-Corruption Organisation of Thailand, the Army had previously commissioned 11 media production projects from the company.
On 23 October, Prachatai received a court summons stating that the company had filed a lawsuit against the Foundation for Community Educational Media (FCEM), which runs Prachatai, its former editor-in-chief Senator Tewarit Maneechai, former FCEM President Dr Kasem Sirisampan, and three other people who shared the news article, for defamation by publication and bringing into a computer system and sharing false information in violation of the Computer Crimes Act.

data.title: Thailand bans new Routledge textbook on contemporary politics, citing national security threats
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Thailand bans new Routledge textbook on contemporary politics, citing national security threats
The Thai police have ordered a ban on the second edition of the Routledge Handbook of Contemporary Thailand, claiming that it contains chapters that could affect national security or cause unrest.
Edited by exiled academic Pavin Chachavalpongpun, the book contains chapters on the Thai military, the monarchy, and the use of the royal defamation law, as well as chapters on popular movements and other social and political issues. Pavin posted on Facebook on Thursday (5 November) that the book was banned for its content about the monarchy.
In a previous post, he wrote that book banning doesn’t work in the age of the internet, since people can buy e-books instead of hard copies. He also wrote that the ban would help promote the book.
Under the 2007 Printing Recordation Act, importing the book for distribution carries a prison sentence of up to three years, or a fine of up to 60,000 baht, or both. The police may also seize and destroy the book.
This is the second time one of Pavin’s publications has been banned in Thailand. In July 2023, the Thai authorities ordered a ban on his book “Rama X: The Thai Monarchy under King Vajiralongkorn” even before it was released.
iLaw noted that the police have banned six books since the Printing Recordation Act came into effect, all of which concerns the monarchy. Other than the two books by Pavin, the list includes:
Thailand’s Crisis and the Fight for Democracy by Giles Ungpakorn A Kingdom in Crisis by Andrew McGregor Marshall The November 2015 issue of the French edition of Marie Claire magazine The article “Thailand: Colossally Popular,” published in The New Age of the Kings: Modern Monarchies in Malaysia and the World

data.title: Detained activist goes on hunger strike to protest bail denial
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Detained activist goes on hunger strike to protest bail denial
Detained Activist Wanwalee Thammasattaya has gone on a hunger strike after she was denied bail and detained pending appeal on a royal defamation charge.
In a message released on her Facebook page, Wanwalee wrote that she has been on a hunger strike since 3 November. She insisted she is not a flight risk as she has attended every court appointment and that she has an uncle with terminal cancer and an elderly grandmother. She wrote that she will not eat until she is granted bail.
Wanwalee is among the five activists sentenced on 30 October to 2 years and 8 months in prison on a royal defamation charge filed against them over speeches given at a protest on 25 November 2020. Wanwalee was denied bail along with activist-turned-reporter Phongsatorn Tancharoen, while the remaining three activists were already detained at the time of the trial.
According to Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR), at least 33 people are detained on a royal defamation charge, 12 of whom are detained pending trial or appeal.

data.title: ECT challenges Supreme Court’s authority to examine Senate candidate qualifications
data.author: eng editor 3
data.summary:
ECT challenges Supreme Court’s authority to examine Senate candidate qualifications
The Election Commission of Thailand (ECT) has sought a Constitutional Court ruling over the Supreme Court’s authority to examine the qualifications of Senate candidates, amid a controversy over the Senate selection fraud.
The ECT commissioners voted 5-2 to petition the Constitutional Court, asking it to rule whether the Supreme Court had the authority to examine the qualifications of five Senate candidates, two of whom are sitting senators, according to several news outlets.
Three petitions were filed with the Supreme Court by unsuccessful Senate candidates, known as reserve senators. They asked the Court to examine the qualifications of five Senate candidates who had passed the preliminary qualification examination conducted by the ECT. The ECT had judged that these candidates were eligible after an earlier petition filed over their qualifications.
The Supreme Court began reviewing the evidence in October 2025. The Court is expected to conclude the case by the end of this year.
However, the majority of the ECT commissioners claim that by accepting the petitions, the Supreme Court has infringed on the ECT’s authority to oversee the Senate selection process, particularly as these candidates had been officially cleared by the commission.
According to the ECT, the Supreme Court has no authority to initiate on its own the process to revisit the ECT’s final decision.
On 4 November, the ECT filed its petition with the Constitutional Court. The ECT argues that the law narrowly defines the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction, and gives it no authority to initiate investigations into electoral fraud, except in cases referred to the Supreme Court by the ECT itself. This includes the case in which the ECT referred to the Court the case of 77 individuals allegedly involved in Senate selection fraud.

data.title: House Speaker rejects petition to proposal to repeal 1976 coup-era order
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
House Speaker rejects petition to proposal to repeal 1976 coup-era order
The House Speaker has rejected a petition initiating a bill to repeal an order made following the military coup of 1976 which increased the penalty for royal defamation.
iLaw reported that the October 6 Memorial Network submitted the petition to the House Speaker on 30 September. On 27 October, House Speaker Sophon Saram of the Bhumjaithai Party rejected the petition, arguing that citizens are not allowed to propose bills that are not related to people’s rights and freedom and this issue is instead a matter of state policy.
The Network said in a Facebook post that the bill, which is backed by over 59,000 people, aims to repeal an order made by the military junta that took power after the 1976 massacre at Thammasat University. It asks the legislature to reconsider an order that increased the penalties for a number of criminal offences, a matter which affects people’s rights and freedom.
The Network argued that penalties for criminal offences are directly related to constitutional rights and freedoms. The Constitution and a 2021 law on bills initiated by citizens requires that a bill be endorsed by at least 10,000 eligible voters before it can be introduced to Parliament. It must also be related in principle to constitutional provisions concerning the people‘s rights and freedoms or the duties of the state; this includes several provisions on the enforcement of criminal law as well as on freedom of expression.
It noted that the 2021 law shows that criminal law is not separate from constitutional freedoms, while the Constitution itself contains provisions controlling the state‘s exercise of its authority in criminal cases. In light of this, setting the penalty for a criminal offence is not solely a matter of state policy but also limits the people’s freedom. data.title: Activist found not guilty of royal defamation over graduation ceremony three-finger salute
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Activist found not guilty of royal defamation over graduation ceremony three-finger salute
The Khon Kaen Provincial Court has dismissed a royal defamation charge filed against activist Songpol “Yajai” Sonthirak for flashing the three-finger salute at a graduation ceremony in December 2022.
Songpol was charged with royal defamation and violation of the Computer Crimes Act for flashing the three-finger “Hunger Games” salute, a well-known resistance symbol used by activists protesting the 2014 military coup and by students in the 2020 pro-democracy movement, after receiving his degree certificate from Princess Sirindhorn, King Vajiralongkorn’s younger sister, during Khon Kaen University’s graduation ceremony on 20 December 2022. He was also charged for an interview with The Isaan Record and another with a Khon Kaen University student activist group. He was indicted in November 2025.
Khon Kaen University reportedly paused its live broadcast of the graduation ceremony while Songpol and subsequent graduates from the Faculty of Law were receiving their certificates, and did not allow comments on the live broadcast after it resumed.
The complaint against him was filed by Kamon Kitkasiwat, leader of a royalist group in Khon Kaen, who was at the time an MP candidate for the royalist Thai Pakdee Party.
Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR) said today (10 November) that the Khon Kaen Provincial Court has dismissed the charge against Songpol. It ruled that, given his behaviour before the ceremony and that he is part of the same activist group as Jatupat Boonpattararaksa, flashing the three-finger salute in front of Princess Sirindhorn can be seen as anti-monarchy, but while it is disrespectful and an insult, it is not defamatory. The princess is also not covered by the royal defamation law, which only covers the King, the Queen, the heir to the throne, and the regent.
